Mechanical Properties of Solids
8
Mechanical Properties of Solids
Why does a steel wire stretch only a little while a rubber band stretches a lot? Stress,
strain, Hooke's law and the three elastic moduli.
KEY IDEA The big idea in one line
Solids are not perfectly rigid. When you apply a force they deform; if they come back to their original shape,
the body is elastic. Stress and strain measure "how hard we push" and "how much it gives"; the ratio of the
two is a property of the material (modulus).

8.1 Elasticity and Plasticity
Elasticity is the property of a body by which it regains its original size and shape when the deforming
force is removed. Plasticity is the opposite: the body does not regain its shape (putty, wet clay, lead).
No real body is perfectly elastic or perfectly plastic; quartz fibr

icity is the opposite: the body does not regain its shape (putty, wet clay, lead).
No real body is perfectly elastic or perfectly plastic; quartz fibre and phosphor-bronze are the closest
to perfectly elastic.
 Atoms joined by "springs" = inter-atomic forces
 Fig 8.1 – Mental model: a solid is a 3-D lattice of atoms joined by spring-like bonds.
ANALOGY The mattress model
Imagine a mattress: balls (atoms) held together by springs (bonds). Pull the mattress and every spring
stretches a bit; let go and they all pull back. If you stretch it too far some springs break or slip – that is
plastic deformation. Tell students: "Elasticity is the spring-ness of the bonds between atoms."

COMMON MISCONCEPTION Steel is MORE elastic than rubber
In everyday language "elastic" means stretchy. In physics a body is more elastic if it needs a larger stress
for the same strain, i.e., it has a larger Young's modulus. Steel (Y ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa) is far more elastic than
rubber. Ask: "Which of the two resists deformation more strongly?" – that is the more elastic one.

ANALOGY Spring constant vs Young's modulus
A thick, short steel rod and a thin, long steel rod have the same Y but very different spring constants (k =
YA/L). Y is like the "quality of steel"; k is like "how stiff this particular spring is". Compare with density vs
mass.

NCEPTION Why does a thicker wire stretch less?
Students often think the material changes. Remind them: Y is the same; the same force is shared by more
area (smaller stress) so the strain is smaller. For a given load, ΔL ∝ 1/r².
EXAM POINTER Applications that appear in board papers
 Cranes use many thin strands twisted into a rope: more flexible, same strength.
 Bridges / beams bend; depression δ = W l³ / (4 b d³ Y) – so use deep (large d) and wide beams.
I-shaped girders save material but keep depth.
 Pillars with distributed (round / hollow) ends bear more load.
 Maximum height of a mountain (~10 km on Earth) is limited by the elastic strength of rock.

strain and elongation. (Y = 2×10¹¹ Pa, g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
› F = mg = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N; A = πr² = π (0.5×10⁻³)² = 7.85×10⁻⁷ m²
› Stress = F/A = 98 / 7.85×10⁻⁷ = 1.25×10⁸ Pa

Mechanical Properties of Fluids

Mechanical Properties of Fluids
Pressure, Pascal's law, flow of fluids, Bernoulli's principle, viscosity and surface tension
– the physics behind hydraulics, aeroplanes, blood flow and raindrops.
KEY IDEA The big idea in one line
A fluid (liquid or gas) cannot resist shear, so it flows. Static fluids are understood through pressure;
moving fluids through conservation of mass (continuity) and conservation of energy (Bernoulli);
real fluids need viscosity; and liquid surfaces behave like a stretched skin (surface tension).

9.2 Streamline Flow, Continuity and Bernoulli's Principle
Streamline (steady/laminar) flow: the velocity at each point does not change with time; every
particle passing a point follows the same path. Streamlines never cross. Turbulent flow is irregular,
with whirlpools (eddies), when speed is high (Re large).

ANALOGY Garden hose and river gorge
Continuity: put your thumb over a hose – the water shoots out faster because the same volume per

Bernoulli – the energy budget: every unit volume of fluid has a fixed "budget" (P + ½ρv² + ρgh). If it
